question: How do hyperscale engineering systems and agent frameworks (Google, Microsoft, AWS, OpenAI, Anthropic, Netflix, Meta, Palantir) implement capability-driven tool selection, dynamic tool scoring, policy gating, and safe fallback routing?
scope: Capability intelligence engines, multi-dimensional scoring matrices, policy evaluation integration, least-privilege provider isolation, and evidence-first execution planning
claims: Capability-driven tool selection decouples abstract task intent from vendor implementations, enabling dynamic scoring based on reliability, cost, latency, and security bounds.
Policy-governed execution planning prevents fallback routes from violating write barriers, authorization scopes, or evidence requirements.
evidence: AWS IAM Policy Engine & Service Control Policies enforce non-bypassable least-privilege boundaries.
Anthropic MCP and OpenAI Tool Choice API demonstrate capability-to-tool signature matching across heterogeneous agent topologies.
observations: Tool scoring must evaluate 12 explicit dimensions: Capability Fit, Compatibility, Reliability, Latency, Cost, Security, Evidence Quality, Reversibility, Availability, Historical Performance, Provider Trust, Permission Fit.
Fallback engines must deterministically evaluate alternative tools without bypassing authorization or security boundaries.
limitations: Initial scoring weights must be marked ASSUMPTION until empirical production telemetry accumulates.
recommendation: Implement Capability Intelligence Engine with 24 formal capability contracts, 12-dimensional tool scoring, policy evaluation gating, and deterministic fallback routing in EOS Control Plane.
